---
title: "Git and GitHub, with an agent"
description: "Log in once with gh, then let the agent do the git commands for you."
---

Your hackathon work lives in a GitHub repository, so you need a
[GitHub account](https://github.com/signup). That matters more than usual here:
the workshop hub is deleted a week after the hackathon, and GitHub is where your
work survives. Git is a lot to learn in one
week, and you do not have to: **your agent can run the git commands for you.**
You make the decisions (what to save, when to share it, and whether a change is
right), and the agent types the commands.

To do that, the agent needs to reach GitHub as you. You set that up once, with
`gh auth login`.

## Why `gh auth login`?

`gh` is GitHub's command-line tool, and it is already installed on the hub.
Logging in with it does two things:

- **`git` can push and pull** over HTTPS without asking you for a password,
  because `gh` stores the credential for it.
- **`gh` itself** can open pull requests, read issues and check on a repository.
  Agents use it all the time.

Everything the agent does through `gh` is done **in your name**, so decide how
much it can reach.

## Choose how much access

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Token for one repository (safer)

The agent can push to your hackathon repository and nothing else.

1. Go to <https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new>.
2. **Token name:** `JupyterHub agent, IOOS hackathon`.
   **Expiration:** a few days after the hackathon.
3. **Repository access:** *Only select repositories*, then pick your project
   repository.
4. **Repository permissions:** set **Contents**, **Pull requests** and
   **Issues** to *Read and write*. Leave the rest at *No access*.
5. Click **Generate token** and copy it. GitHub shows it only once.

Then, in a terminal, run `gh auth login` and answer:

- **Where do you use GitHub?** GitHub.com
- **Preferred protocol?** HTTPS
- **Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials?** Yes
- **How would you like to authenticate?** Paste an authentication token

### Full access

The agent can do anything you can on GitHub, in every repository you can reach,
including private ones.

In a terminal, run `gh auth login` and answer:

- **Where do you use GitHub?** GitHub.com
- **Preferred protocol?** HTTPS
- **Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials?** Yes
- **How would you like to authenticate?** Login with a web browser

It prints a one-time code. Open the link, paste the code, and approve.

:::

Check that it worked:

```bash
gh auth status
```

## Tell git who you are

Commits need a name and an email. Do this once:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

Use the email on your GitHub account. If you would rather keep it private, use
the `noreply` address shown at <https://github.com/settings/emails>.

## Let the agent do git

Ask for the outcome you want, not the command. For example:

| You want to… | Say to the agent |
|---|---|
| Get a copy of a repository | *"Clone github.com/ocean-icechunks/2026-ioos-hackathon into my home folder."* |
| See what you changed | *"What have I changed since the last commit?"* |
| Save your work | *"Make a new branch and commit these changes with a clear message."* |
| Share it | *"Push the branch and open a pull request. Explain what changed in the description."* |
| Catch up with your team | *"Pull the latest changes from main and tell me what is new."* |
| Recover from a mess | *"Git says there is a merge conflict. Explain what happened before you fix anything."* |

Three habits keep this safe:

- **Work on a branch, and merge through a pull request.** Ask the agent never to
  push to `main`.
- **Read the change before it is committed.** Ask *"show me the diff"* if the
  agent does not.
- **Never let credentials into a commit.** Keys and tokens belong in
  environment variables or in a file listed in `.gitignore`. The
  ocean-icechunks skill already insists on this.

## Learn the basics anyway

It helps to know what the agent is doing on your behalf: clone, commit, push
and pull. The NMFS HackDays lesson
[Basic Git/GitHub skills in the terminal](https://nmfs-opensci.github.io/NMFSHackDays-2025/topics-skills/02-git-terminal.html)
walks through all four in about 20 minutes. Or ask your agent to explain each
command as it runs it.
